summary: Specified a DKIM adjunct called Author Domain Signing Practices, letting a domain publish how it signs mail so receivers could judge messages lacking a valid signature from the author's domain. It is now historic.

eli5.summary: A school says on its website, 'all our letters have our stamp'. That helped others spot unstamped fake letters. The idea is now retired.

questions: where is the adsp record published
subtitle: A DNS record that let a domain announce that it signs all its mail with DKIM, so receivers could judge unsigned messages. Now Historic.

tldr.problem: A DKIM signature proves a domain vouches for a message, but a missing signature does not prove forgery. Domains that sign everything had no way to say so.
tldr.mechanism: ADSP publishes a DNS TXT record at _adsp._domainkey.DOMAIN with dkim=unknown, all or discardable. A receiver looks it up for the From domain when a message has no valid signature from that domain.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5617 is now Historic and has been updated by RFC 8553, so it should not be treated as a current mechanism.

today: RFC 5617 was a Standards Track document but is now Historic, and RFC 8553 updates it. Do not treat ADSP as a current mechanism.

sections.title: What ADSP Is For
sections.content:
DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) lets a domain sign messages so recipients can verify them with a public key published in DNS. But the absence of a signature is not an a priori indication of forgery, and early on most mail would be unsigned.

Some domains might sign all outgoing mail, for example to protect their brand names, and may want to advertise that. Author Domain Signing Practices (ADSP) is the mechanism for that: a machine-readable record published by the domain of an Alleged Author, which a receiver can look up in an ADSP check. The basic requirements are in RFC 5016, and the document assumes familiarity with RFC 4871.

An Author Address is an address in the From: header, the Author Domain is the part after the @, and an Author Domain Signature is a valid DKIM signature whose d= domain equals the Author Domain.
sections.eli5: A company tells the world, 'we put our seal on every letter'. Then, if a letter shows up without the seal, you can be suspicious.

sections.title: How a Receiver Uses ADSP
sections.content:
ADSP matters most when a message has no valid signature, because then the ADSP result is directly relevant. If the message has an Author Domain Signature, ADSP adds nothing for that domain. If it carries a valid signature from another domain, the receiver can weigh both. With several Author Addresses, lookups SHOULD be done independently on each.

A lookup gives one of four results:

  • messages might or might not carry an Author Domain Signature (the default when the domain exists but has no ADSP record);
  • all messages are signed with an Author Domain Signature;
  • all messages are signed and are discardable: the domain encourages recipients to discard unsigned ones;
  • the domain is out of scope because it does not exist in DNS.

A temporary DNS failure can end the lookup with no result at all. ADSP has no effect unless some external system acts on the verdict, for example by treating the message differently or showing an indicator to the recipient.
sections.eli5: When a letter arrives without a seal, you check what the sender said about their letters: 'maybe sealed', 'always sealed', or 'always sealed, and please throw away unsealed ones'.

sections.title: The ADSP Record and Lookup
sections.content:
ADSP records are DNS TXT records at the Author Domain prefixed with _adsp._domainkey., for example _adsp._domainkey.domain.example. They use the tag=value syntax from RFC 4871 with whitespace in place of folding whitespace. Every record MUST start with the dkim= tag, whose value is unknown, all or discardable. Any other value is treated as unknown, and unrecognized tags MUST be ignored. ADSP applies to one domain, not its subdomains, and domains MUST NOT publish ADSP records with wildcard names.

The lookup procedure first checks scope: the host MUST query DNS for the Author Domain itself, and if that returns NXDOMAIN the domain is out of scope. A NODATA answer is not the same as NXDOMAIN. Then the host MUST query the TXT record. A single valid record is used. NXDOMAIN or no records means there is no ADSP record. More than one record, or an invalid one, makes the result undefined. A SERVFAIL ends the algorithm without a result, and the message might be queued or answered with a temporary SMTP error.
sections.eli5: The note is kept in a special drawer in the domain's address book. First check that the address exists, then open the drawer and read the one note inside.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Cautions
sections.content:
The threat is malicious senders passing themselves off as an Author they are not authorized to send for. The RFC admits there is no empirical evidence of how much this contributes to recipient deception, or that closing it will have a significant effect. Checkers can also be drawn into traffic multiplication attacks on domains named in fraudulent mail.

DNS wildcards at or above a domain interfere with the scope check, so a domain using a practice other than unknown SHOULD NOT publish wildcard records. DNS attacks are addressed by DNSSEC.

The appendices warn that mailing lists, forwarders and other paths can modify messages and invalidate a signature. A domain SHOULD NOT publish discardable if it wants to maximise delivery. A domain with independent users and liberal use policies should publish only unknown. A domain that sends no mail can safely publish discardable. Third-party signing is not addressed.
sections.eli5: Telling people to throw away unsealed letters is risky, because good letters can lose their seal on the way, like when a mailing list re-wraps them.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
ADSP created two IANA registries: the ADSP Specification Tag Registry, with dkim as its initial entry, and the ADSP Outbound Signing Practices Registry, with unknown, all and discardable. New values require a published RFC after IETF Review.

It also adds a dkim-adsp method to the Email Authentication Method Name Registry, with results such as none, pass, unknown, fail, discard, nxdomain, temperror and permerror, for use in Authentication-Results header fields.
sections.eli5: It adds new names to the official list so everyone writes the same words in their notes.

items.label: Unknown
items.desc: The domain might sign some or all email.

items.label: All
items.desc: All mail from the domain is signed with an Author Domain Signature.

items.label: Discardable
items.desc: All mail is signed, and unsigned mail should be discarded.
